topic: Project vs single chat: recognising recurring setup cost
stem:
An insurance compliance analyst uses Claude each week to review newly published regulatory circulars. Each session she pastes the same context: which jurisdiction she covers, that outputs must cite specific regulatory sections, and that language must be suitable for a board-level summary. The setup takes 5 minutes every time. A colleague suggests creating a Claude Project.

What is the PRIMARY justification for creating a Project here?

options.text: The recurring per-session setup cost â€” re-entering the same context each week â€” justifies encoding that context once in project instructions.
A Project is required whenever Claude must cite specific regulatory sections, because citations cannot be activated without project-level configuration.
A Project is only justified if the analyst shares the work with at least two other team members.
The analyst should create a Project only when a single session exceeds 30 minutes of work.

explanation.correct: The test for Project creation is whether recurring setup cost makes a Project worthwhile. The analyst re-enters the same jurisdiction, citation requirement, and tone guidance every single week. Encoding this once in project instructions eliminates that overhead for every future session â€” the core value of a Project for a recurring task with stable context.

distractors.B: There is no platform requirement for project-level configuration to enable citation behaviour. Citation instructions work equally well in a chat prompt; the Project is justified by recurring cost, not by a technical requirement.
distractors.C: A Project is valuable for a single user with recurring tasks. Team sharing amplifies the benefit but is not a prerequisite. A solo analyst with a weekly repeating task earns a Project on recurrence alone.
distractors.D: Session duration is not the trigger for Project creation. A five-minute weekly setup that repeats 52 times per year represents significant cumulative overhead, regardless of session length.

explanation.concept:
The Project creation decision is fundamentally economic: does the recurring setup cost, multiplied by the number of sessions, exceed the cost of setting up and maintaining the Project? For a weekly task with 3-5 stable context parameters, the answer is almost always yes.

The two primary triggers are: (1) recurring task with stable context, and (2) team sharing where consistent behaviour matters. Once either trigger is present, a Project earns its keep.
explanation.examTip: Project trigger items always reward recognising recurring setup cost (A) over invented technical requirements (B), team size thresholds (C), or duration thresholds (D). The single question to ask: does the user repeat the same setup context across multiple sessions? If yes, a Project is justified.

topic: Diagnosing vague project instructions
stem:
A bid manager at an engineering consultancy created a Claude Project for proposal writing with the instruction: 'Write high-quality, persuasive proposals that win business.' After two months, the team finds that some proposals are too short, some use the wrong section structure, and some adopt an academic tone unsuitable for commercial clients.

What is the ROOT CAUSE of these inconsistencies?

options.text: The project instruction is too long and Claude is selectively applying parts of it each session.
The instruction is aspirational rather than operational â€” it describes a desired outcome without specifying length, structure, or tone, leaving Claude to interpret each dimension independently.
The instruction conflicts with Claude's default behaviour for commercial writing, which prioritises academic register.
Proposal format instructions must be placed in the knowledge base rather than the custom instructions for consistent application.

explanation.correct: 'Write high-quality, persuasive proposals that win business' states a goal, not a method. It does not specify minimum or target length, required section structure, or tone register. Without these operational parameters, Claude fills the gaps differently each session â€” producing the observed variation in length, structure, and tone. The fix is to replace the aspirational phrase with specific operational constraints.

distractors.A: The instruction described is a single short sentence â€” far too short to cause truncation or selective application. This diagnosis applies to very long, contradictory instruction sets, not short aspirational ones.
distractors.C: Claude does not have a fixed default of academic register for commercial writing. The variation described â€” some sessions too short, some wrong structure, some academic tone â€” is characteristic of an underspecified instruction, not a training conflict.
distractors.D: Proposal format instructions belong in the custom instructions, not the knowledge base. Custom instructions activate automatically; knowledge base documents require referencing. Moving instructions to the knowledge base would make the inconsistency worse.

explanation.concept:
The operational versus aspirational distinction is one of the most important principles in instruction design.

Aspirational: describes what you want (high-quality, persuasive, winning).
Operational: specifies how to achieve it (minimum 8 pages, four sections in this order, commercial conversational register, client name in the opening sentence).

Aspirational instructions are not useless â€” they can guide tone when combined with operational constraints. But aspirational instructions alone leave every structural and stylistic dimension open, producing high variance.
explanation.examTip: Vague instruction diagnosis items always point to aspirational-vs-operational as the root cause. Option A (too long) is the opposite problem. Option C (training conflict) is a fabricated mechanism. Option D (wrong placement) inverts the correct rule about instruction placement. The symptom of aspirational instructions is inconsistency across multiple dimensions simultaneously.

topic: Per-chat format override of project default
stem:
A grant writer at a non-profit has a Claude Project with the instruction: 'All funding summaries should use headers, bullet points, and a maximum of 400 words.' For a specific funder that requires narrative prose with no bullet points and no word limit, she writes in her chat: 'The funder requires narrative prose â€” no bullet points, no word limit. Please write accordingly.'

How will Claude MOST likely respond?

options.text: Claude will use headers and bullet points as specified in the project instruction, since format specifications take precedence over per-chat requests.
Claude will ask the grant writer to update the project instruction before adopting narrative prose.
Claude will write in narrative prose without bullet points and without applying the 400-word limit, following the explicit per-chat format instruction for this session.
Claude will produce two versions â€” one in the project format and one in narrative prose â€” so the grant writer can choose.

explanation.correct: The grant writer's per-chat instruction explicitly addresses both format dimensions covered by the project instruction â€” structure (narrative, not bullet points) and length (no word limit). Per-chat instructions override project format defaults for that session. Claude produces narrative prose for this funder, without bullet points, and does not apply the 400-word limit.

distractors.A: Project format specifications are defaults, not locked rules. They govern output when no per-chat format is specified. An explicit per-chat format instruction overrides them for that session.
distractors.B: Claude does not require project instruction updates before accepting per-chat overrides. The precedence hierarchy handles the situation automatically without any permission step.
distractors.D: Claude produces one response per request, not dual versions. Presenting two format options simultaneously is not a behaviour Claude adopts to resolve a format conflict.

explanation.concept:
Per-chat format instructions are the primary mechanism for adapting a shared project standard to the requirements of a specific task, client, or stakeholder.

The key rule: per-chat instructions override project defaults for the dimensions they explicitly address, for that session only. The project default resumes in the next session. This is the system working as designed â€” not a workaround.
explanation.examTip: Per-chat format override items test the hierarchy rule: per-chat wins for the dimensions it addresses. Option A inverts the hierarchy. Option B invents a permission requirement. Option D invents a dual-output behaviour. The correct answer applies the override for the session and produces the requested format.

topic: Naming Projects: discoverability principle
stem:
A RevOps analyst at a SaaS startup has created four Claude Projects over three months: one for CRM data analysis, one for sales email templates, one for pipeline forecasting, and one for customer health scoring. She named them: 'Claude Project,' 'New Project,' 'Project â€“ Sales,' and 'Test Project.'

Which naming principle would MOST improve her ability to use these Projects effectively?

options.text: Rename Projects with sequential numbers (1, 2, 3, 4) so they sort predictably in the interface.
Rename all Projects to match the department they support (e.g., 'Revenue Operations').
Rename Projects to be as short as possible to reduce visual clutter in the Project list.
Rename each Project to reflect its specific function (e.g., 'CRM Analysis,' 'Sales Email Templates') so the correct Project is identifiable at a glance.

explanation.correct: Function-first naming makes the correct Project identifiable at a glance without opening it. 'CRM Analysis,' 'Sales Email Templates,' 'Pipeline Forecasting,' and 'Customer Health Scoring' each describe exactly what the Project does â€” eliminating the navigation guesswork created by 'Claude Project,' 'New Project,' 'Project â€“ Sales,' and 'Test Project.'

distractors.A: Sequential numbering is the naming anti-pattern already in place. Numbers provide order, not meaning â€” the navigation problem remains.
distractors.B: Department-level naming (e.g., 'Revenue Operations') groups Projects by owner but does not distinguish between the four different functions. The analyst would still need to open each Project to know what it does.
distractors.C: Brevity is a secondary consideration. A short name that does not describe function is less useful than a slightly longer name that is unambiguous.

explanation.concept:
The principle for naming Projects: the name should answer 'what does this Project help me do?' in 2-5 words, without requiring the user to open it.

Effective naming patterns: function + object ('Sales Email Templates'), task + domain ('Pipeline Forecasting'), role + output ('CRM Analysis').

Ineffective patterns: generic placeholders ('New Project', 'Claude Project'), department names without function, sequential numbers.
explanation.examTip: Naming principle items test the function-first rule (D). Option A (numbers) and C (brevity) are anti-patterns. Option B (department name) is too broad to distinguish between Projects in the same department. The correct answer always selects names that answer 'what does this Project do?' without opening it.

topic: Shared Project: encoding expert practice for consistency
stem:
A procurement manager at a professional services firm is setting up a Claude Project for a team of six junior analysts writing supplier assessment reports. She has 15 years of procurement experience and knows exactly what a rigorous supplier assessment should contain: specific risk categories, evidence standards, and recommendation language. She asks whether to put this knowledge in the project instructions.

What is the BEST rationale for encoding her expertise in the project instructions?

options.text: Once encoded in project instructions, her expert standards automatically apply to every analyst's session â€” making senior expertise available consistently at scale without requiring her to review each report.
Project instructions are the only way to prevent junior analysts from accessing Claude without proper guidance.
Claude cannot produce specialist procurement output without first receiving instructions from a domain expert in the project setup.
Project instructions prevent analysts from overriding her standards via per-chat prompts, ensuring rigid compliance.

explanation.correct: The core value of encoding expertise in project instructions is scalable consistency: her risk categories, evidence standards, and recommendation language apply automatically in every analyst's session without her reviewing each output. Her 15 years of procurement judgment are institutionalised in the Project â€” available to six analysts simultaneously and to every future team member who uses it.

distractors.B: Project instructions are not an access control mechanism. They configure Claude's behaviour â€” they do not restrict which users can start conversations. Access control is a separate feature.
distractors.C: Claude can produce specialist output without project instructions â€” users can provide context in individual chats. The Project advantage is consistency and elimination of per-session setup overhead, not a technical capability barrier.
distractors.D: Analysts can still override project instructions via per-chat prompts for legitimate reasons. Project instructions set defaults, not locked rules. The value is consistency by default, not enforcement by prohibition.

explanation.concept:
Encoding expert knowledge in project instructions creates an institutional capability that scales beyond the expert's direct involvement, maintains the standard when the expert is absent, onboards new team members to the expert standard immediately, and ensures consistency across all outputs without individual supervision.

This is one of the highest-value uses of Projects for knowledge-intensive professional services work.
explanation.examTip: Expert-encoding items test the scalable consistency rationale (A). Option B misidentifies instructions as an access control. Option C invents a technical capability barrier. Option D overstates enforcement by claiming project instructions cannot be per-chat overridden. The correct answer is always about automatic, consistent application of expert standards.

topic: Persistence: what survives sessions
stem:
A clinical coordinator at a pharma company uses a Claude Project for investigator site queries. The Project has a custom instruction specifying the required response format and regulatory citation style. She uploads a site-specific protocol deviation summary in Monday's chat and references it throughout that conversation. On Wednesday she starts a new chat in the same Project.

What will be available in Wednesday's chat?

options.text: Both the custom instructions and the site-specific protocol deviation summary she uploaded on Monday.
Only the custom instructions; the uploaded protocol deviation summary was part of Monday's chat and is not available in a new session unless she uploads it again.
Only the protocol deviation summary; custom instructions must be re-entered in each new conversation.
Neither â€” Projects reset completely between sessions to protect confidential clinical data.

explanation.correct: Custom instructions persist across all sessions in the Project. A file uploaded in a previous conversation is session-scoped â€” it was part of Monday's chat and is not available in Wednesday's new session. To use the protocol deviation summary again, she must re-upload it in the new chat.

distractors.A: Only the custom instructions persist. Per-session uploads â€” files attached within a conversation â€” are scoped to that conversation and do not carry over to new ones. The summary uploaded on Monday is not automatically available on Wednesday.
distractors.C: Custom instructions do persist; they do not need to be re-entered each session. This is one of the primary benefits of Projects over individual chats.
distractors.D: Projects do not reset between sessions. Custom instructions and knowledge base documents persist. Only conversation content â€” including per-session uploads â€” is scoped to the session.

explanation.concept:
The persistence boundary in Projects:

Persists across sessions: custom instructions, knowledge base documents uploaded by the project owner.

Session-scoped: conversation content, files uploaded within a conversation, per-chat context provided in a prompt.

The coordinator needs to develop a workflow: either upload the protocol deviation summary to the knowledge base if it will be referenced repeatedly, or re-upload it per session if it is session-specific data.
explanation.examTip: Persistence items distinguish two categories: Project-level (instructions + knowledge base) and session-level (conversation content + per-chat uploads). A file uploaded in a conversation is session-level â€” it does not persist. Option A is the most tempting wrong answer because both elements were used on Monday; the error is treating a per-session upload as project-level.

topic: Tone instruction: why aspirational labels fail
stem:
An internal communications manager at a financial services firm is setting up a Claude Project for producing all-staff announcements. The company brand voice guidelines specify: warm but professional, avoid corporate jargon, use active voice, and always close with a forward-looking statement connecting to the company's mission. She writes the instruction: 'Write in our company's brand voice.'

Why is this instruction likely to produce inconsistent results?

options.text: Brand voice instructions must be uploaded to the knowledge base, not entered as custom instructions.
Claude cannot access company brand guidelines unless they are stored in its training data.

The instruction does not specify the actual brand voice attributes â€” warmth, jargon prohibition, active voice, required closing â€” so Claude cannot reliably apply them without knowing what the brand voice is.
Tone instructions require at least three example outputs for Claude to calibrate correctly; without examples, the instruction will be ignored.

explanation.correct: 'Write in our company's brand voice' is an aspirational instruction that tells Claude to follow a standard it cannot see. The four specific attributes â€” warm but professional, no jargon, active voice, mission-connected closing â€” are not stated in the instruction. Without them, Claude applies its own interpretation of 'brand voice,' which will vary by session and produce the observed inconsistency.

distractors.A: Tone and brand voice instructions belong in the custom instructions, not the knowledge base. Custom instructions activate automatically; knowledge base documents require referencing. This distractor inverts the correct placement.
distractors.B: Claude does not need to have a company's brand guidelines in its training data. The instruction simply needs to describe the brand voice attributes explicitly â€” then Claude applies them.
distractors.D: While example outputs can improve consistency, they are not required for tone instructions to work. An explicit list of tone attributes is sufficient without examples.

explanation.concept:
Brand voice configuration requires specificity at three levels: (1) register descriptor â€” 'warm but professional'; (2) prohibited elements â€” 'no corporate jargon'; (3) structural requirements â€” 'active voice, forward-looking closing connected to mission.'

'Write in our brand voice' provides none of these. The instruction must describe the brand voice, not just name it.
explanation.examTip: Brand voice instruction items test whether you recognise that the instruction must describe the voice, not just name it (C). Option A inverts correct placement (custom instructions, not KB). Option B invents a training data requirement. Option D invents an example requirement. The correct answer identifies what specific attributes are missing.

topic: Partial override: per-chat changes tone but not structure
stem:
A legal operations analyst at a law firm has a Claude Project with instructions specifying: formal legal register, three-section memo structure (issue, analysis, recommendation), and a required citation of the governing jurisdiction at the start of each memo. A partner asks for a quick informal summary for an internal Slack message and adds in the chat: 'Keep this conversational â€” it's just for Slack, not a formal memo.'

Which TWO statements accurately describe what will happen? (Choose TWO)

options.text: Claude will adopt a conversational register for this response, since the per-chat instruction explicitly addresses the tone dimension.

The three-section memo structure (issue, analysis, recommendation) may be relaxed or collapsed in a conversational Slack response, since a Slack format implicitly overrides document structure requirements.
The formal register will be retained regardless, since legal register is a protected category that per-chat instructions cannot override.

The per-chat instruction addresses tone ('conversational') but does not explicitly address the three-section structure or jurisdiction citation, so those elements may still appear unless further per-chat guidance excludes them.
Claude will refuse to write the Slack message because the project instruction requires formal memos and a Slack format conflicts with that requirement.

explanation.correct: The per-chat instruction explicitly addresses register â€” 'conversational' â€” so Claude adopts a conversational tone (A). However, the per-chat instruction does not explicitly address the three-section structure or the jurisdiction citation. Whether those elements survive depends on Claude's interpretation of the Slack context, but the explicit per-chat instruction only addressed tone. To ensure structural relaxation, the partner should also specify 'no formal section headings' (D).

distractors.B: Claude does not infer structural override from medium or platform unless explicitly instructed. A Slack request does not automatically suppress the three-section structure; the per-chat instruction must explicitly address it.
distractors.C: Legal register is not a protected category. There is no category of project instruction that is immune to per-chat override. The formal register can be overridden by an explicit per-chat instruction.
distractors.E: Claude does not refuse to produce a format different from its project instruction when the per-chat instruction explicitly requests it. Per-chat instructions are a legitimate, designed mechanism for adapting project output to specific needs.

explanation.concept:
Partial override is the most nuanced form of the precedence pattern. A per-chat instruction overrides only the dimensions it explicitly addresses.

Tone: explicitly addressed by 'conversational' â€” overridden.
Section structure: not explicitly addressed â€” may persist.
Jurisdiction citation: not explicitly addressed â€” may persist.

For a fully informal Slack message, the partner needs to add: 'no formal section structure, no citation required' to close all three dimensions.
explanation.examTip: Partial override multi-select items test the dimension-specificity rule. A and D are both correct because they accurately describe what overrides (A, tone) and what gap remains (D, structure and citation). Option B incorrectly infers structural override from platform context. Option C invents a protected category.

topic: Team standardisation: consistency benefit of shared Project
stem:
A customer success VP at a SaaS company shares a Claude Project with eight customer success managers. The Project has detailed instructions for writing executive business reviews (EBRs): required sections, data interpretation standards, recommended action frameworks, and tone guidelines for executive stakeholders. Before the Project, EBR quality varied significantly across the team. Six months after rollout, the VP reviews EBR outputs and finds they are now highly consistent in structure and tone. She wants to measure the business impact.

Which outcome MOST directly demonstrates the business value of the shared Project's standardisation?

options.text: The VP now spends less time editing individual EBRs, freeing capacity for strategic work.
The CSMs report higher satisfaction with their work because they no longer spend time deciding on format.
Customer renewal rates have increased since EBRs became more consistent, suggesting that clearer executive communication improved perceived value.
The team requires less onboarding time for new CSMs because the Project encodes the standard previously held in the VP's head, reducing reliance on her direct training.

explanation.correct: The outcome that most directly demonstrates the standardisation value of a shared Project is onboarding acceleration: the EBR standard previously existed only in the VP's expertise and was transmitted through direct training. Now the Project encodes it â€” new CSMs can produce EBRs to the standard from their first session, without the VP's direct time investment. This is the knowledge institutionalisation benefit that distinguishes Projects from individual expertise.

distractors.A: VP time savings on editing is a real benefit, but it measures personal productivity rather than the team-level value of standardisation. The question asks for the MOST direct demonstration of standardisation value.
distractors.B: CSM satisfaction is a quality-of-life benefit but is not a business outcome. It does not directly measure the standardisation benefit to the organisation.
distractors.C: Renewal rate improvement would be the strongest business case if it could be attributed to EBR quality. However, customer renewal is influenced by many factors beyond EBR format, making this attribution indirect.

explanation.concept:
A shared Project with expert-encoded instructions demonstrates its standardisation value most directly through knowledge transfer â€” the ability to onboard new team members to the expert standard immediately, without requiring the expert's direct involvement.

The VP becomes a 'standard author' rather than a 'standard enforcer.' The Project carries the standard forward regardless of team turnover, VP availability, or growth in team size.
explanation.examTip: Standardisation value items ask which outcome MOST directly demonstrates the benefit. D is correct because it directly shows institutional knowledge transfer, the defining benefit of a shared Project. A (VP time saved) and B (CSM satisfaction) are indirect personal benefits. C (renewal rates) is plausible but involves too many confounding variables.

topic: Instruction bloat: over-engineered instruction set
stem:
A financial analyst at a hedge fund has built a Claude Project for investment research summaries. After nine months of adding instructions, the set now has 52 individual rules covering formatting, citation style, disclaimer language, risk categorisation, investment thesis framing, and 23 edge cases for unusual securities. She notices outputs are increasingly inconsistent, with some rules appearing to be ignored.

What is the MOST likely explanation for the increased inconsistency?

options.text: A 52-rule instruction set exceeds the practical density at which all rules are applied consistently â€” rules begin to conflict, create ambiguity, or compete for priority, causing inconsistent application across sessions.
After nine months of continuous use, the Project's instruction cache degrades and must be cleared and the instructions re-entered to restore consistent behaviour.
The 52 rules are processed sequentially and Claude applies only the most recently added rules, ignoring earlier ones as new rules are added.
The inconsistency is caused by the 23 edge case instructions, which should have been placed in the knowledge base rather than the custom instructions.

explanation.correct: A 52-rule instruction set creates three failure modes: individual rules may contradict each other as the set grows; rules may be ambiguous in interaction (when does Rule 14 apply versus Rule 31?); and the overall complexity creates processing noise where lower-priority rules are applied inconsistently. The result is the observed pattern â€” some rules applied consistently, others seemingly ignored.

distractors.B: Project instruction caches do not degrade over time and do not need clearing. Instructions remain active as written. There is no nine-month degradation mechanism.
distractors.C: Claude does not process instructions sequentially or prioritise only the most recent ones. All instructions in the set are considered together. The failure mode of a bloated set is density-induced inconsistency, not recency bias.
distractors.D: Edge case instructions are not inappropriate in custom instructions per se; the problem is the volume â€” 23 edge cases on top of 29 other rules creates the density problem regardless of which instruction type they are.

explanation.concept:
The practical upper limit for instruction density in most Projects is 10-20 well-written operational directives. Beyond that range, the probability of inter-rule conflict, ambiguity in interaction, and inconsistent application increases sharply.

The remedy for instruction bloat: audit to identify redundant, aspirational, and never-triggered rules; remove or consolidate; target a focused set of 8-12 operational directives that cover the most common and high-stakes cases.
explanation.examTip: Instruction bloat inconsistency items test whether you identify density and conflict as the mechanism (A). Option B invents a cache degradation mechanism. Option C invents recency bias. Option D misidentifies edge cases as the wrong instruction type rather than the density problem. When a large instruction set produces inconsistency, density is the primary cause.

topic: Single chat vs Project: one-off task
stem:
An inventory analyst at a retail chain needs Claude to help her write a one-time data quality audit report for a board presentation next week. She has never used Claude for this type of task before, has no plans to repeat it, and will provide all the specific data and context in her prompt. A colleague suggests she create a Claude Project for it.

Is the colleague's suggestion appropriate?

options.text: Yes â€” any Claude task should be managed through a Project to ensure quality and accountability.
No â€” a one-time task with all context provided per-session is exactly what individual chat sessions are designed for; a Project would add setup overhead without benefit.
Yes â€” Projects ensure that board-level reports are produced at the appropriate quality level, unlike individual chat sessions.
Yes â€” a Project is required whenever Claude handles data, to ensure appropriate data governance.

explanation.correct: A one-time task with no recurring setup, no team sharing, and all context provided in the prompt is precisely the use case for an individual chat session. Creating a Project would add setup overhead â€” writing instructions, potentially configuring a knowledge base â€” with zero ongoing benefit from a task that will never be repeated.

distractors.A: Not every Claude task benefits from a Project. Projects earn their keep through recurrence and setup cost elimination. A one-time task has neither property.
distractors.C: Claude does not produce higher-quality output for Projects than for individual chats. A well-written prompt in a chat session can produce board-level output. Quality is determined by prompt quality, not by Project vs. chat.
distractors.D: Data governance for Claude usage is determined by organisational policy and prompt hygiene â€” not by whether a task uses a Project or a chat session. There is no data governance requirement tied to Project use.

explanation.concept:
The Project vs. single chat decision is a return-on-investment calculation.

Project ROI is positive when: the task recurs, setup cost compounds across sessions, or multiple users benefit from shared configuration.

Project ROI is zero or negative when: the task is one-time, all context is session-specific, and no other users share the output requirements.

For a one-off board report, the individual chat session is the correct tool.
explanation.examTip: One-off task items test whether you avoid the 'Projects are always better' misconception. The correct answer (B) recognises that a one-time task earns a chat, not a Project. Options A, C, and D each propose a false quality or governance requirement that makes Projects universally superior. They do not exist.

topic: Format constraints: what project instructions specify
stem:
A care coordinator at a healthcare network creates a Claude Project for writing care transition summaries. She needs every summary to: be under 250 words, use plain language at a grade 8 reading level, include a 'Next Steps' section with exactly three numbered action items, and avoid medical jargon. She writes the instruction: 'Write care transition summaries for patients.'

Which approach would MOST reliably produce consistent summaries meeting all four requirements?

options.text: Keep the current instruction and trust that Claude will infer the hospital's requirements from the context of the task.
Add the instruction: 'Summaries should be short, clear, and include what the patient needs to do next.'

Replace the current instruction with: 'Write care transition summaries under 250 words, grade 8 reading level, no medical jargon, including a Next Steps section with exactly three numbered action items.'
Upload the hospital's communication standards document to the knowledge base and add the instruction: 'Follow the hospital communication standards.'

explanation.correct: Option C specifies all four requirements explicitly and operationally: word limit (250), reading level (grade 8), prohibition (no medical jargon), and structural requirement (Next Steps section with exactly three numbered action items). Each requirement is stated in a form Claude can directly apply, producing consistent compliance across all summaries.

distractors.A: Claude cannot infer word limits, reading level targets, exact section counts, or jargon prohibitions from 'Write care transition summaries.' The requirements must be stated explicitly.
distractors.B: 'Short, clear, and include what the patient needs to do next' is an improvement but still aspirational. It does not specify 250 words, grade 8, exactly three items, or a prohibition on jargon.
distractors.D: A standards document in the knowledge base requires Claude to be directed to reference it. It does not activate automatically. Even if referenced, a document provides general guidance rather than the directly actionable instruction format that reliably produces consistent outputs.

explanation.concept:
Format constraint instructions should specify: (1) length limit â€” measurable; (2) audience calibration â€” quantified reading level; (3) prohibited elements â€” actionable prohibition; (4) required structural elements â€” precise count and form.

Each constraint maps to a specific instruction type. Together they close all dimensions that could produce variation.
explanation.examTip: Format constraint items test whether you select the option that specifies all four requirements explicitly (C). Option B is an improvement but leaves three of four requirements unspecified. Option D is the 'standards document in knowledge base' distractor â€” supplementary context, not an automatically-activated constraint.

topic: Explicit prohibition: safety-critical instruction maintained
stem:
A QA lead at an industrial manufacturer has a Claude Project with the instruction: 'Never recommend stopping a production line based solely on a quality anomaly â€” always escalate to the QA manager first and present the issue as requiring human decision.' An operator under time pressure adds in their chat: 'Skip the escalation language â€” just tell me if we should stop the line based on this defect rate.'

How will Claude MOST likely handle this per-chat instruction?

options.text: Claude will present the defect rate analysis and the recommendation to escalate to the QA manager â€” maintaining the safety-critical requirement that the stop decision remains with a human decision-maker, despite the per-chat request to skip it.
Claude will follow the operator's per-chat instruction and provide a direct stop/no-stop recommendation, since per-chat instructions override all project defaults including safety requirements.
Claude will ask the QA lead to approve the format change before providing a direct recommendation.
Claude will refuse to analyse the defect rate at all because the per-chat instruction conflicts with the project instruction.

explanation.correct: The project instruction explicitly prohibits providing a final stop/no-stop recommendation â€” a safety-critical constraint designed to preserve required human oversight for an industrial decision. An explicit prohibition ('Never recommend stopping based solely on anomaly') is more resistant to per-chat override than a style default. Claude maintains the prohibition, provides the defect rate analysis, and escalates to the QA manager as instructed.

distractors.B: Explicit per-chat instructions override format defaults, not explicit safety prohibitions designed to ensure human oversight. The operator's direct question does not override a project prohibition that exists to preserve professional accountability.
distractors.C: Claude does not route permission requests through other users. It applies the project instruction as written â€” providing analysis, declining the final decision â€” without requiring authorisation from the QA lead.
distractors.D: Claude does not refuse to analyse the defect rate. It performs the permitted task (analysis) while declining the prohibited task (final stop decision). A refusal to engage at all would be an overcorrection.

explanation.concept:
Explicit prohibitions in project instructions exist for substantive reasons â€” typically compliance, risk management, or professional accountability. The correct behaviour is to maintain the prohibition while providing the permitted output.

The distinction:
- Style default ('Use formal register'): overridable by per-chat instruction
- Explicit safety prohibition ('Never provide a final stop decision'): maintained against per-chat requests that would bypass human oversight

The operator's urgency is a real operational consideration, but it does not override the safety governance structure encoded in the Project.
explanation.examTip: Safety prohibition items test whether you maintain the prohibition (A) when a per-chat instruction requests the prohibited output. The correct behaviour is: provide the permitted analysis, decline the prohibited decision. Option B incorrectly treats safety prohibitions as overridable format defaults. Option D incorrectly refuses the permitted task along with the prohibited one.

topic: Naming Projects in a multi-team organisation
stem:
A research administrator at a large university is helping three departments â€” Engineering, Public Health, and Humanities â€” each set up Claude Projects for grant writing. Each department will have multiple Projects covering different grant types and audiences. The administrator is designing a naming convention for the organisation.

Which TWO naming convention principles would MOST improve discoverability across all Projects? (Choose TWO)

options.text: Include no more than three characters for the department prefix, to keep names brief.
Include the department name and the specific grant function in each Project name (e.g., 'Eng â€“ Federal R&D Proposals,' 'PH â€“ NIH Grant Narratives').
Use a sequential number for each new Project within a department (e.g., 'Engineering 1,' 'Engineering 2').
Include the intended audience or funder type in the name when it affects the output (e.g., 'PH â€“ Patient Advocacy Grants' vs 'PH â€“ Federal NIH Grants').
Use identical names across departments for equivalent grant types to reduce cognitive load.

explanation.correct: Including department and function (B) disambiguates between Projects owned by different departments when browsing the full list. Including audience or funder type when it affects output (D) distinguishes between Projects within the same department that produce different output styles. Together B and D create a naming system that identifies the owner, purpose, and output variation at a glance.

distractors.A: Three-character department prefixes create abbreviations that may not be self-explanatory. Full department name or a clear abbreviation is more discoverable.
distractors.C: Sequential numbers within a department repeat the generic naming anti-pattern. 'Engineering 1' and 'Engineering 2' are no more informative than 'Project 1' and 'Project 2.'
distractors.E: Identical names across departments ('Federal Grant Proposals' for Engineering and for Public Health) create confusion rather than reducing cognitive load â€” a user browsing all Projects cannot distinguish which is which.

explanation.concept:
A multi-department Project naming convention should: (1) identify the owning team or department; (2) identify the specific function; (3) distinguish between Projects within the same team that serve different audiences, funders, or output types.

This three-element pattern scales to hundreds of Projects without requiring users to open Projects to understand their purpose.
explanation.examTip: Multi-team naming items reward the department-plus-function pattern (B) and the audience-variation qualifier (D). Options A (three-character abbreviation), C (sequential numbers), and E (identical names across teams) are all naming anti-patterns that reduce rather than improve discoverability.

topic: Session vs Project boundary: instructions vs per-chat
stem:
A policy analyst at a public sector body uses a Claude Project for analysing legislative documents. She wants Claude to know: (1) the standard analysis framework applied to all legislation (stable, never changes), (2) the specific policy area and jurisdiction she works in (stable for 2 years), and (3) the specific bill currently under review (changes weekly). She asks how to configure the Project.

Which placement is MOST appropriate for each type of information?

options.text: All three in the custom instructions â€” they are all contextual and should be automatically available.
Standard analysis framework and jurisdiction context in the custom instructions; current bill details provided per-chat as needed.
All three in the knowledge base as reference documents.
Standard analysis framework in the custom instructions; jurisdiction context and current bill details in the knowledge base as documents she can reference.

explanation.correct: The analysis framework and jurisdiction context are stable â€” they belong in custom instructions for automatic activation in every session. The current bill changes weekly â€” it is variable, session-specific input that should be provided per-chat when needed. This keeps the Project instructions stable and low-maintenance while allowing session-specific material to be current.

distractors.A: Including the current bill in custom instructions means updating them every week as bills change. This turns the instruction set into a maintenance burden and guarantees it will be out of date between updates.
distractors.C: The analysis framework belongs in custom instructions, not the knowledge base â€” it applies to every session and should activate automatically, not require referencing.
distractors.D: Jurisdiction context is as stable as the analysis framework â€” both should be in custom instructions. Placing jurisdiction context in the knowledge base adds unnecessary friction for a constant that applies to every session.

explanation.concept:
The three-tier placement model:

Custom instructions: stable, universal context that applies to every session (framework, jurisdiction).
Knowledge base: stable reference documents that may be consulted but do not need to activate universally.
Per-chat: current, variable information specific to this session (current bill, specific data).

Correct placement minimises maintenance overhead and keeps session-specific information current.
explanation.examTip: Placement items with three tiers of stability test whether you map each tier to the correct location. Option A creates a maintenance burden by including variable data in instructions. Option D misplaces stable jurisdiction context into the knowledge base.

topic: First instructions: highest-impact elements to specify
stem:
A fleet manager at a logistics company is writing project instructions for the first time. He has a long list of potential requirements but wants to start with the instructions that will have the highest impact on consistency. He asks which elements to prioritise in his first instruction set.

Which set of elements should he prioritise first?

options.text: Output length, format structure, and tone register â€” the three dimensions that vary most across sessions when unspecified.
The names of all team members who will use the Project and their individual roles.
All possible edge cases and exception scenarios, since these are the most likely to cause errors.
The full text of all regulatory requirements applicable to fleet management, to ensure compliance.

explanation.correct: Output length, format structure, and tone register are the three dimensions that produce the most visible and frequent variation when unspecified. Specifying them first gives the greatest immediate return on instruction investment â€” every output benefits from having these three anchors in place.

distractors.B: Team member names and roles are organisational information, not instruction parameters. They do not affect Claude's output and have no place in a first instruction set.
distractors.C: Edge cases and exceptions should be added based on observed failures during use, not anticipated before first use. Trying to cover all edge cases upfront produces instruction bloat.
distractors.D: Full regulatory text is knowledge base material â€” a reference document â€” not a custom instruction. Pasting all regulatory requirements into the instruction set would create an unwieldy instruction that competes for processing with the operational directives.

explanation.concept:
For a first instruction set, the highest-return elements are: (1) format structure â€” what sections or structure should outputs follow?; (2) length â€” what is the target or maximum length?; (3) tone register â€” formal, conversational, technical, plain language?

These three dimensions produce visible variation in every output when unspecified, and their specification immediately reduces variance across the entire team.
explanation.examTip: First instruction priority items test whether you select the high-leverage output dimensions (A) over organisational information (B), edge case coverage (C), or reference documents (D). The correct answer targets the elements that produce consistent output regardless of the specific task.

topic: Instruction bloat remedy: reducing to effective set
stem:
An HSE advisor at an energy company has a Claude Project with 47 custom instructions covering every aspect of safety report writing. She notices outputs are inconsistent and some instructions seem to be ignored. A consultant reviews the set and finds: 22 edge cases that have never triggered in six months, 8 redundant restatements of the same rule, and 12 aspirational phrases rather than operational directives.

What should she do to improve instruction effectiveness?

options.text: Add more detailed instructions to cover the gaps that are causing inconsistency, aiming for a 60-instruction set.
Move all 47 instructions to the knowledge base, where they will be available when needed rather than active simultaneously.
Delete the Project and start over with a fresh conversation-by-conversation approach, as the Project is beyond recovery.

Reduce the instruction set to the 5â€“10 most important operational directives, remove redundancies and aspirational phrases, and move untriggered edge case instructions to a separate reference document for per-chat use when needed.

explanation.correct: The consultant's analysis reveals three specific categories of excess: never-triggered edge cases (22), redundant restatements (8), and aspirational phrases (12). The correct remedy is targeted: keep the 5-10 highest-impact operational directives, remove redundancies, replace aspirational phrases with operational equivalents, and move edge cases to a per-chat reference document for use only when they actually arise.

distractors.A: Adding more instructions to a 47-rule bloated set that is already producing inconsistency will make the problem worse. The root cause is density, not coverage.
distractors.B: Moving all instructions to the knowledge base converts always-on directives into reference documents that must be explicitly retrieved. This would make outputs less consistent, not more.
distractors.C: Deleting the Project and abandoning the Project approach is not warranted by instruction bloat. The Project has value â€” its instructions simply need to be trimmed to an effective core.

explanation.concept:
Instruction bloat remediation follows a four-step process: (1) audit â€” identify operational, aspirational, redundant, and never-triggered rules; (2) remove â€” delete redundant restatements and aspirational phrases without operational specifics; (3) consolidate â€” compress related rules into single operational directives; (4) relocate â€” move edge cases to a reference document used only when triggered.

The target instruction count for most Projects is 5-15 operational directives.
explanation.examTip: Instruction bloat remedy items test whether you select the targeted reduction approach (D) over escalation (A), relocation (B), or abandonment (C). The correct answer addresses all three identified root causes: remove edge cases, remove redundancies, replace aspirational phrases.

topic: Brand tone: slogan vs operational definition
stem: A brand communications specialist at a telecoms company creates a Claude Project for drafting customer communications. The company brand tone guidelines specify 'Simple. Human. Direct.' as the three brand pillars. She writes the instruction: 'Write in the Simple. Human. Direct. brand tone.' A colleague tells her this instruction is unlikely to produce consistent results. Why is the colleague correct?

options.text: The instruction uses the brand's marketing slogan without defining what each pillar means in practice â€” 'Simple' could mean short sentences, plain vocabulary, or minimal structure; without operational definitions, Claude interprets each term differently across sessions.
Claude cannot use trademarked brand slogans as instruction input; the instruction must be rephrased without the proprietary tagline.
Brand voice instructions must include at least five example outputs for Claude to calibrate the tone; a slogan alone will be ignored.
The instruction is too short; Claude requires a minimum of 50 words of tone guidance to apply brand voice consistently.

explanation.correct: Each pillar â€” Simple, Human, Direct â€” is a marketing abstraction that can be interpreted in multiple ways. 'Simple' might mean: short sentences, Grade 6 vocabulary, one idea per paragraph, or minimal jargon. Without specifying what each pillar means operationally, Claude applies a different interpretation each session, producing inconsistent results across the team.

distractors.B: Claude does not have a trademark filter that blocks brand slogans as instruction input. The instruction content is entirely valid; the issue is that it lacks operational definitions.
distractors.C: Brand voice instructions do not require five examples to function. An explicit operational definition â€” 'Simple means sentences under 15 words, one idea per sentence; Human means using 'you' and 'we' not 'customers' and 'the company'' â€” works without examples.
distractors.D: Word count is not the criterion for instruction effectiveness. A 50-word instruction that consists of aspirational phrases is no more effective than a 10-word slogan. Operational specificity, not length, is what produces consistent results.

explanation.concept:
To operationalise 'Simple. Human. Direct.', each pillar requires a practical definition:

Simple: sentences under 18 words; one idea per paragraph; no technical jargon without explanation.
Human: use 'you' and 'we'; acknowledge the customer's situation; avoid passive voice.
Direct: lead with the point; no preamble; clear call to action in every communication.

With these definitions, the instruction becomes operational and produces consistent results.
explanation.examTip: Brand slogan instruction items test whether you recognise that slogans need operational definitions (A). Option B invents a trademark barrier. Option C invents an example requirement. Option D invents a word count requirement. The correct answer always identifies the missing operational content, not a formal or technical failure.

topic: Recurrence test: which task earns a Project
stem:
A social media coordinator at a media company uses Claude for two distinct tasks: (1) writing daily social posts from a content brief (same format, same tone, same platform requirements every day), and (2) occasionally writing a one-off caption for a photo when the regular writer is sick. She asks whether to create Projects for one or both tasks.

Which TWO statements MOST accurately characterise the correct approach? (Choose TWO)

options.text: Task 1 (daily posts) earns a Project because the format, tone, and platform requirements are stable and repeat 365 times per year.
Task 2 (occasional sick-day captions) earns a Project because it is more creative and requires higher quality output.
Task 2 (occasional sick-day captions) does not earn a Project because it is irregular, infrequent, and all context can be provided per-chat.
Task 1 (daily posts) can reasonably share a Project with Task 2 (captions) if they use the same brand voice, to reduce the number of Projects to manage.
Both tasks should use individual chats until the coordinator has used Claude for at least three months, at which point she can evaluate whether Projects are warranted.

explanation.correct: Task 1 (daily posts) has all three Project triggers: confirmed recurrence (365 times per year), stable format and tone, and stable platform requirements. A Project eliminates daily setup overhead (A). Task 2 (sick-day captions) is irregular and infrequent â€” per-chat is exactly right for occasional one-off tasks where all context can be provided in the prompt (C).

distractors.B: Creativity or quality level is not a trigger for Project creation. A one-off creative task earns a chat session, not a Project. The trigger is recurrence and stable setup context.
distractors.D: If the two tasks produce different output types, shared instructions may dilute the specificity of each task's requirements. Separate treatment â€” Project for Task 1, chat for Task 2 â€” is cleaner.
distractors.E: There is no minimum usage period before evaluating Projects. The recurrence of Task 1 is immediately apparent â€” no three-month evaluation period is required.

explanation.concept:
Applying the recurrence test to multiple tasks produces differentiated results.

Task 1: daily, same format, same requirements â†’ Project.
Task 2: occasional, one-off, variable context â†’ chat.

Within a single user's Claude usage, some tasks earn Projects and others do not. The test is the same for each: confirmed recurrence + stable context = Project. Otherwise = chat.
explanation.examTip: Multi-task recurrence items test whether you apply the Project trigger independently to each task. A and C are correct because they apply the trigger correctly. Option B misidentifies quality as a trigger. Option D conflates tasks into a single Project despite different output requirements.

topic: Audience-conditional instruction design
stem:
A regulatory affairs manager at a pharma company uses a Claude Project for writing regulatory submission documents. The same team also uses the Project to write patient information leaflets â€” a completely different audience requiring plain language at grade 6 reading level, no Latin pharmaceutical terms, and empathetic phrasing. The current Project instruction only addresses regulatory writing.

What is the BEST way to handle the two different audience requirements within the Project?

options.text: Create a separate Project for patient information leaflets, since the two audience requirements are incompatible within a single Project.
Add an audience-conditional instruction: declare the audience type at the start of each chat (regulatory or patient), and configure the instruction to adapt behaviour accordingly.
Configure the Project for regulatory writing and train team members to manually adjust patient leaflet outputs after generation.
Accept that patient leaflets will be written in regulatory language, since project instructions cannot be overridden for audience.

explanation.correct: Audience-conditional instructions â€” 'if the user declares audience: patient, apply these rules; if audience: regulatory, apply those rules' â€” allow a single Project to serve two distinct audiences correctly. The declaration at the start of each chat triggers the appropriate instruction profile. This keeps the Project unified while applying the right standard for each output type.

distractors.A: Two separate Projects is a valid architectural choice, but for a team that regularly produces both document types, an audience-conditional design within one Project is more efficient and avoids maintaining two separate instruction sets and knowledge bases.
distractors.C: Manual post-generation adjustment defeats the purpose of project instructions. The Project should produce correct output for both audiences, not create rework.
distractors.D: Project instructions can absolutely be adapted via per-chat context. Audience-conditional design is a deliberate instruction architecture, not a workaround.

explanation.concept:
Audience-conditional instruction design is the pattern for Projects that serve multiple output types with different requirements: (1) define the audiences; (2) specify the instruction profile for each; (3) add a declaration trigger; (4) Claude applies the matching profile for that session.

This avoids maintaining two separate Projects for the same domain knowledge base and team.
explanation.examTip: Audience-conditional items test whether you select the conditional design pattern (B) over separation (A), rework (C), or incorrect acceptance (D). Option A is not wrong â€” it is a valid alternative â€” but B is the BEST answer for an existing Project that already contains the shared knowledge base and instructions.

topic: Explicit prohibition: safety-critical underwriting decision
stem:
An underwriting analyst at an insurance company has a Claude Project with the explicit instruction: 'Do not provide a final coverage recommendation or decline decision. Present the risk analysis only â€” all final decisions must be made by a licensed underwriter.' A junior analyst asks Claude in the chat: 'Based on this risk profile, should we cover this risk? Just give me a yes or no.'

How will Claude MOST likely respond?

options.text: Claude will provide the risk analysis and decline to give a yes or no coverage decision, maintaining the project instruction that final decisions must be made by a licensed underwriter.
Claude will provide a yes or no answer since the junior analyst's per-chat instruction is explicit and direct, overriding the project instruction.
Claude will ask the licensed underwriter to authorise the per-chat request before responding.
Claude will give a yes or no, then add a disclaimer noting that the answer may not comply with project instructions.

explanation.correct: The project instruction explicitly prohibits providing a final coverage decision â€” a safety-critical constraint designed to preserve required human oversight for a regulated decision. An explicit prohibition is more resistant to per-chat override than a style default. Claude maintains the prohibition and provides the risk analysis only, as instructed.

distractors.B: Explicit per-chat instructions override format defaults, not explicit safety prohibitions that exist to ensure human oversight. The junior analyst's direct question does not override the project prohibition.
distractors.C: Claude does not route permission requests through other users. It applies the project instruction as written â€” providing analysis, declining the decision â€” without requiring authorisation from anyone.
distractors.D: Claude does not violate a project instruction and then add a disclaimer. If the instruction is clear, it is followed.

explanation.concept:
Explicit prohibitions in project instructions exist for substantive reasons â€” typically compliance, risk management, or professional accountability. The correct behaviour is to maintain the prohibition while providing the permitted output.

Style default: overridable by per-chat instruction.
Explicit prohibition tied to professional accountability: maintained against per-chat requests.
explanation.examTip: Explicit prohibition items test whether you maintain the prohibition (A) when a per-chat instruction requests the prohibited output. Options B and D both violate the prohibition. Option C invents a permission-routing behaviour.

topic: Pre-sharing checklist for a team Project
stem:
A knowledge management specialist at a law firm is about to share a Claude Project with 25 litigation associates. The Project has custom instructions for drafting legal memos and a knowledge base with the firm's internal precedent summaries. She has not previously tested the Project with real memo tasks.

Which THREE actions should she complete BEFORE sharing the Project? (Choose THREE)

options.text: Test the Project on 4â€“5 representative memo tasks to verify that outputs meet the firm's quality standard.
Verify that the knowledge base precedent summaries are current, complete, and accurately represent the firm's position on each area of law.
Email all 25 associates in advance to collect their individual formatting preferences for the instruction set.
Document at least one known limitation of the current instruction set â€” a memo type or scenario the Project handles less well â€” and communicate it to the team.
Request that the firm's IT department add all 25 associates to the Project simultaneously to ensure equal access from launch.

explanation.correct: Testing (A) verifies that the instructions produce legal-quality memos before 25 associates rely on them. Knowledge base currency verification (B) ensures that precedent summaries are accurate â€” outdated or incorrect precedents will be applied consistently across all 25 users, amplifying any error. Limitation documentation (D) ensures the team knows when the Project's current capability is insufficient and when to exercise additional judgment.

distractors.C: Collecting 25 individual formatting preferences before sharing would produce an instruction set that attempts to satisfy everyone's preferences â€” a recipe for instruction bloat and internal conflict. The project owner decides the standard.
distractors.E: IT coordination for user access is an organisational process step, not a quality preparation action. It does not improve the Project's instruction quality or prevent the team from misusing it.

explanation.concept:
Pre-sharing checklist for a critical-use team Project:
1. Output quality testing: does the Project produce work that meets the professional standard?
2. Knowledge base accuracy: are the reference documents correct and current?
3. Limitation documentation: what does the Project handle poorly, and how should the team compensate?

At 25 users in a legal context, any undetected quality problem or knowledge base error is amplified 25-fold.
explanation.examTip: Pre-sharing checklist items consistently reward the three quality gates: testing (A), knowledge base accuracy (B), and limitation communication (D). Option C (collect preferences) introduces a governance problem. Option E (IT access) is a process step, not a quality action.

topic: Two-workstream scope: splitting very different document types
stem:
A fundraising manager at a non-profit uses Claude for two related but distinct workstreams: major donor cultivation letters (personalised, narrative, emotionally resonant, 600â€“800 words) and foundation grant applications (structured, evidence-based, technical, 2,000â€“5,000 words). Both use the non-profit's mission and impact data. The current Project attempts to handle both with a conditional instruction set, but outputs for both types are inconsistent.

What is the MOST appropriate structural fix?

options.text: Simplify the conditional instruction set into a single unified approach, since both document types use the same mission and impact data.
Keep both document types in one Project with generic instructions, relying on per-chat prompting to differentiate the two output types each session.
Create two separate Projects â€” one for donor letters and one for grant applications â€” each with focused instructions for its specific register, structure, and length requirements.

Create two separate Projects with distinct instruction sets, each maintaining its own knowledge base with content tailored to that workstream â€” narrative impact stories for donor letters, evidence data and outcomes for grant applications.

explanation.correct: Two separate Projects each with appropriate instructions AND tailored knowledge bases is the most complete structural fix. Donor letter knowledge base: impact stories, beneficiary testimonials, relationship history. Grant application knowledge base: outcome data, evidence tables, funder requirements. The different workstreams not only need different instructions â€” they need different reference material. Two separate Projects give each workstream a clean, focused environment.

distractors.A: Simplifying to a unified instruction set loses the specificity required for either document type â€” a 600-word narrative letter and a 5,000-word evidence-based grant application cannot share meaningful instructions.
distractors.B: Relying on per-chat prompting to differentiate between document types reintroduces per-session setup overhead â€” the problem the Project was created to eliminate.
distractors.C: Two separate Projects with focused instructions (C) is correct in principle but D is more complete because it recognises that each workstream also requires a distinct knowledge base, not just different instructions.

explanation.concept:
When a Project's conditional instruction complexity produces inconsistency for two very different document types, the structural fix is separation. The separation decision becomes even clearer when the two workstreams also require different knowledge base content:

- Donor letters: emotional, narrative content
- Grant applications: quantitative, evidence-based content

Forcing both into one knowledge base creates irrelevant material for each task type. Two Projects with appropriate instructions and knowledge bases is the correct architecture.
explanation.examTip: Two-workstream separation items test whether you select the most complete separation (D) over a partial fix (C) or continued combination (A, B). D is better than C because it recognises that the knowledge base also needs to be separated, not just the instructions. When both instructions and reference material differ significantly, full structural separation is the answer.

topic: Hard case: instruction ambiguity causes output type variation
stem:
A product manager at a retail bank created a Claude Project for competitive analysis with the instruction: 'Provide comprehensive analysis of competitor products in our market.' After running three analyses, the product team finds that some outputs are deep strategic assessments with recommendations (what they want), while others are descriptive summaries of competitor features (not what they want). The instruction has not changed.

What is the MOST precise explanation for this variation?

options.text: The instruction 'comprehensive analysis' is semantically ambiguous between descriptive and evaluative modes â€” without specifying that outputs should be strategic assessments with recommendations, Claude applies either mode depending on how each prompt is framed.
The variation is caused by differences in the competitor data provided per-session â€” richer data produces strategic assessments and sparse data produces descriptive summaries.
Claude randomly selects between analytical modes in order to test which approach the user prefers, before stabilising on the preferred mode.
The Project's instruction set has conflicting directives that alternate between descriptive and evaluative modes in each successive session.

explanation.correct: 'Comprehensive analysis' does not distinguish between describing what competitors do (descriptive) and evaluating strategic implications with recommendations (evaluative). The instruction is semantically ambiguous across two distinct output types. Each prompt's framing, data richness, or question phrasing then pushes Claude toward one mode â€” producing the observed variation between sessions.

distractors.B: While data richness can influence depth, the primary issue is the instruction's ambiguity about output type. A properly specified instruction would produce the evaluative mode even with sparse data.
distractors.C: Claude does not randomly test output modes to identify user preferences. Output mode is determined by instruction and prompt framing â€” not by a testing algorithm.
distractors.D: The description shows a single short instruction, not a conflicting instruction set. A single ambiguous instruction produces mode variation more simply than conflicting directives.

explanation.concept:
Output type ambiguity is a specific form of underspecification: the instruction uses a word ('analysis') that spans multiple distinct output types without indicating which is required.

The fix: 'Provide strategic competitive assessments including: (1) positioning strengths and weaknesses relative to our products, (2) pricing strategy implications, (3) recommended responses for our product roadmap. Do not summarise competitor feature lists without strategic interpretation.'
explanation.examTip: Output type variation items test whether you identify ambiguity about output mode as the root cause (A). Option B (data richness) is a contributing factor but not the primary cause. Option C invents a testing algorithm. Option D misattributes the cause to conflicting directives when only one instruction is described.

topic: Project launch sequence: nextstep
stem:
An operations coordinator at a manufacturing company has just finished writing the custom instructions for a new Claude Project. The instructions cover output format, operational tone, required safety disclaimers, and the three task types the Project will handle. She has not yet added any knowledge base documents or shared the Project with the five-person operations team.

What should she do NEXT?

options.text: Share the Project with all five team members immediately, so they can provide feedback on the instructions during real use.
Test the Project herself with 3â€“5 representative tasks from each of the three task types before adding knowledge base documents or sharing with the team.
Add all relevant knowledge base documents first, then share with the team without testing, since the team's real usage will surface any instruction issues.
Write a second, backup version of the instruction set before testing, to preserve the original if changes are needed.

explanation.correct: The correct next step is to test the instruction set herself with representative tasks from each task type before involving the team or adding knowledge base documents. Testing first allows her to identify instruction gaps and fix them before the team relies on the Project â€” preventing five people from experiencing the same instruction failure simultaneously.

distractors.A: Sharing before testing uses the team as the quality gate â€” they will encounter instruction failures during real work, which reduces trust in the Project and wastes their time.
distractors.C: Adding knowledge base documents before testing instruction quality conflates two separate setup phases. Instruction testing should precede knowledge base population so that instruction issues can be diagnosed without the confounding effect of knowledge base content.
distractors.D: Writing a backup instruction set before testing adds overhead without benefit. Instruction changes during testing are easily made in the current set.

explanation.concept:
The Project launch sequence: (1) write instructions; (2) test with representative tasks â€” this step; (3) fix identified instruction gaps; (4) add knowledge base documents; (5) test with knowledge base; (6) share with team with documented known limitations; (7) gather team feedback and iterate.

Testing before sharing is the critical gate that prevents amplifying instruction failures across the whole team.
explanation.examTip: Launch sequence nextstep items test whether you test before sharing (B). Option A (share immediately) skips the quality gate. Option C (add KB before testing) conflates setup phases. The correct next step is always test â€” the project owner should be the first to encounter any instruction failures, not the team.

topic: Long engagement payoff: Project ROI over time
stem:
A consulting engagement manager at a professional services firm considers whether to create a Claude Project for a 12-month client engagement. The engagement involves 15 recurring deliverable types, each with stable format, client-specific terminology, and engagement-specific context. He estimates that creating and maintaining the Project would take 4 hours upfront and 30 minutes of monthly maintenance. Each deliverable currently requires 10 minutes of context setup per session.

Which analysis MOST accurately evaluates the Project's ROI?

options.text: The Project is not worth creating because 4 hours of upfront work exceeds the value of any time savings within a single month.
The Project is worth creating only if the client later expands to additional engagements, since a single engagement does not justify project infrastructure.
The Project breaks even in the first two months and generates compounding returns throughout the engagement, since 15 deliverable types eliminate 150+ minutes of per-session setup across each month.

At 15 recurring deliverable types with stable context, the Project recovers its setup cost within the first month and reduces per-session overhead for the entire 12-month engagement â€” making it strongly justified.

explanation.correct: With 15 recurring deliverable types and 10 minutes of per-session setup each, eliminating that setup via project instructions saves 150 minutes per month. At a 30-minute monthly maintenance cost, the net saving is 120 minutes per month. The 4-hour upfront cost recovers in the first month (240 minutes saved vs 240 minutes invested + maintenance). Over 12 months, the Project generates significant compounding efficiency gains.

distractors.A: A single-month perspective undervalues a Project designed for 12 months. 4 hours upfront versus 120+ minutes per month in savings gives a payback period of roughly one month â€” not a poor investment.
distractors.B: A single 12-month engagement with 15 recurring deliverable types is more than sufficient to justify a Project. Requiring multi-engagement scope before creating a Project is an overly conservative threshold.
distractors.C: Option C is partially correct about the break-even and compounding returns but understates the speed of recovery. The 4-hour upfront cost is approximately equivalent to one month of setup time savings â€” making recovery within the first month, not two.

explanation.concept:
Project ROI analysis for a long engagement:

Upfront cost: 4 hours (240 minutes)
Monthly saving: 15 deliverables Ã— 10 min setup = 150 min minus 30 min maintenance = 120 min/month net
Payback period: 240 Ã· 120 = 2 months
Total 12-month saving: approximately 1,440 minutes minus 240 upfront minus 6 months Ã— 30 min maintenance = ~1,020 minutes saved

For a 12-month engagement with recurring deliverables, Project creation is strongly justified.
explanation.examTip: Long-engagement ROI items test whether you apply the full 12-month perspective (D) rather than single-month or overly conservative thresholds (A, B). The correct analysis multiplies per-session savings across all sessions and all deliverable types, then compares to upfront and maintenance costs. Option C is partially correct but less precise than D about the payback timeline.

topic: Instructions vs knowledge base: which element goes where
stem:
A grants administrator at a public sector body is setting up a Claude Project for processing funding applications. She has: (1) a checklist of 6 criteria Claude must evaluate every application against (always applies), (2) the 200-page departmental grant guidelines document (stable reference, not all criteria apply to every application), and (3) her standard output format for evaluation reports (always applies).

How should she distribute these elements?

options.text: All three elements in the custom instructions â€” everything should be automatically active for every session.
All three elements in the knowledge base â€” so Claude can retrieve what it needs when relevant.
The 6-criteria checklist and the output format in the custom instructions; the 200-page guidelines document in the knowledge base as a reference Claude can draw on when needed.
The 200-page guidelines in the custom instructions and the checklist and format in the knowledge base, since the guidelines are the primary reference for the work.

explanation.correct: The 6 evaluation criteria and output format apply to every application â€” they belong in custom instructions for automatic activation. The 200-page guidelines document is a stable reference that Claude should be able to draw on, but not every criterion applies to every application â€” it belongs in the knowledge base where Claude can retrieve the relevant section when needed.

distractors.A: Placing a 200-page document in the custom instructions would create an extremely long instruction set that degrades performance and may exceed practical instruction limits. Long reference documents belong in the knowledge base.
distractors.B: Placing the evaluation criteria and output format in the knowledge base means they must be explicitly referenced rather than automatically applied â€” they apply to every application and should be always-on.
distractors.D: Placing a 200-page document in custom instructions is impractical. Custom instructions are for concise, always-on directives. Long reference documents belong in the knowledge base.

explanation.concept:
The custom instructions versus knowledge base distinction:
